The disease in the image is called apple scab, which is a fungal infection that affects the leaves and fruits of apple trees. It is caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis and can lead to the formation of brown spots, yellowing, and even defoliation of the tree. Apple scab can also cause the fruit to become discolored and deformed.

To treat apple scab, it is essential to practice proper tree care and maintenance. This includes pruning the tree to promote air circulation, removing any affected leaves and fruit, and applying a fungicide to the tree during the early spring and late summer months when the fungus is most active. Additionally, it is crucial to maintain a balanced soil pH and provide adequate nutrients to the tree to support its overall health and resistance to diseases.

The image shows a corn plant with a large, rotten, and moldy head, which is a sign of a disease called "corn smut." Corn smut is caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis and affects the corn plant by causing abnormal growth and deformations in the ears. This disease can lead to significant yield losses and is often considered a major problem in corn production.

To treat corn smut, it is essential to practice proper crop management and preventive measures. These include:

1. Rotation: Rotating the corn crop with other crops can help reduce the risk of infection by breaking the life cycle of the fungus.
2. Resistant varieties: Planting corn varieties that are resistant to corn smut can help minimize the impact of the disease.
3. Proper irrigation and drainage: Ensuring adequate water supply and proper drainage can help prevent the growth of the fungus.
4. Fungicide application: Applying fungicides during the early stages of the disease can help control the spread of the fungus and reduce the severity of the infection.
5. Crop inspection and removal: Regularly inspecting the crop and removing any affected plants can help prevent the spread of the disease.

By implementing these measures, farmers can effectively manage corn smut and protect their crop from significant yield losses.
